Compression · Field and archive (B ∪ A)theopheastus

Theophrastus was Aristotle's colleague and successor at the Lyceum, a philosopher and naturalist of whose writings less than a tenth survives; on a reading proposed against the received one, the two names do not mark two distinct authors, and the number of makers is open.

👤 The received person

  • Born Tyrtamus, Eresos, c. 371; reputedly renamed by Aristotle for his speech.2↘
    Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school.§1 Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech.§2
  • Successor: Aristotle's library and the school; some 35 years as head.1↘
    Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his own will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to be held in common and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus.§3
  • The will: garden and buildings to the school; the books to Neleus.1↘
    Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his own will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to be held in common and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus.§3

📚 The works

  • 227 titles listed; a small fraction survives.1↘
    Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis.§4
  • Plants: Enquiry and Causes, the counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; 'father of botany'.1↘
    The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany.§5
  • Characters, logic, senses: thirty types; prosleptic syllogisms credited to him; On the Senses an independent work.1↘
    The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work.§6
  • Metaphysics: difficulties for teleology and the unmoved mover.1↘
    His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them.§7

⚖️ How far from Aristotle

  • Only partly determinable: neither footnote nor radical innovator; much known through Alexander and Simplicius.1↘
    How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius.§8

🔁 One corpus, two names (proposed)

  • Not two distinct authors: the corpora do not support treating the names as two author-variables; maker count open.1↘
    A body of work set against that received picture holds that the surviving corpora under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus do not support treating the names as two distinct authors; the number of makers is left open, open because uncounted, and calendar and membership are not claimed.§9
  • The hinge, read: the fragment's sections 6–7 continue Λ from inside; no second-person marker.1↘
    Against the received reading of the Metaphysics as a pupil's questions put from outside to Aristotle's Λ, its sixth and seventh sections are read as a hinge written from inside Λ, with no marker at the hinge of a second person taking up a first person's work; at one locus the fragment names Λ 8's object, the number of the spheres, and refuses by name the method Λ has used.§11
  • Ranked first: fragment → Λ, first of 1,482 directed edges; the sequence cannot decide which came first.1↘
    A directed measure of rare-term uptake ranks the edge from the fragment to Λ first of 1,482; the two passages are read as standing in ordered dependency at eight locations, and the sequence alone is held unable to decide which was written first.§12
  • Catalogues: twelve shared titles; 'Aristotelian or Theophrastan'; five ghost twins.1↘
    Twelve titles stand letter for letter in both catalogues, one entry assigns a work to "Aristotelian or Theophrastan", and five of Aristotle's lost early dialogues have Theophrastan twins.§13

🧪 Measured

  • Axis, read: world against apparatus, ahead of author.1↘
    The first principal axis of stylistic variation across the two corpora is read as a world/apparatus axis, ahead of any author axis; supervised attribution recovers the names above chance (0.798, against 0.860 for the operation), an earlier claim that they sit at chance was withdrawn, and no such separation is taken to license an inference to distinct makers.§15
  • Names recovered: 0.798 against 0.860; 'at chance' withdrawn; no inference to makers.1↘
    The first principal axis of stylistic variation across the two corpora is read as a world/apparatus axis, ahead of any author axis; supervised attribution recovers the names above chance (0.798, against 0.860 for the operation), an earlier claim that they sit at chance was withdrawn, and no such separation is taken to license an inference to distinct makers.§15

🔍 The witness

  • Read as void as a control: no attestation independent of style, doctrine or succession; the witnesses to the Plato/Aristotle split pass through him.1↘
    Theophrastus is also read as void as an independent control for Aristotle: he fails the rule that a control be attested independently of style, doctrine or succession, the two corpora share one transmission channel, and all four kinds of witness to the division between Plato and Aristotle are read as passing through him.§14
  • Strongest form, a hypothesis: one self-dividing maker.1↘
    The strongest form, one self-dividing maker, with Plato the dialogue position, Theophrastus the first draft and Aristotle the treatise position and legal identity, is stated as a hypothesis.§17

⚠️ Falsifiers and limits

  • Would weaken or decide it: a second-voice sign at the hinge; an independent witness; Isḥāq's Arabic at five loci.1↘
    These readings state what would weaken or decide them: a grammatical sign at the hinge, or an extant Theophrastan work answering the fragment's questions, would falsify the hinge; an independent witness to the partition from outside the Peripatos would weaken the witness reading; Isḥāq's Arabic, read at five loci, would decide among the competing readings of the fragment; and any epigraphic or papyrological item for Theophrastus is listed as still open.§18
  • Provisional: no independent uptake; whether he was a person left open.1↘
    What they show concerns what Theophrastus's attestation rests on, and leaves open whether he was a person; they are held as provisional, with no independent uptake.§19

Theophrastus

Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school. Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech.

Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his own will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to be held in common and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus. Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis.

The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany. The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work. His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them.

How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius.

A body of work set against that received picture holds that the surviving corpora under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus do not support treating the names as two distinct authors; the number of makers is left open, open because uncounted, and calendar and membership are not claimed. On that reading the received biography is a set of relations supplied by receiving texts, and "Theophrastus" is read as a position within the corpus, the first draft of the Aristotle-position, "first" naming the order of method. Against the received reading of the Metaphysics as a pupil's questions put from outside to Aristotle's Λ, its sixth and seventh sections are read as a hinge written from inside Λ, with no marker at the hinge of a second person taking up a first person's work; at one locus the fragment names Λ 8's object, the number of the spheres, and refuses by name the method Λ has used. A directed measure of rare-term uptake ranks the edge from the fragment to Λ first of 1,482; the two passages are read as standing in ordered dependency at eight locations, and the sequence alone is held unable to decide which was written first. Twelve titles stand letter for letter in both catalogues, one entry assigns a work to "Aristotelian or Theophrastan", and five of Aristotle's lost early dialogues have Theophrastan twins. Theophrastus is also read as void as an independent control for Aristotle: he fails the rule that a control be attested independently of style, doctrine or succession, the two corpora share one transmission channel, and all four kinds of witness to the division between Plato and Aristotle are read as passing through him. The first principal axis of stylistic variation across the two corpora is read as a world/apparatus axis, ahead of any author axis; supervised attribution recovers the names above chance (0.798, against 0.860 for the operation), an earlier claim that they sit at chance was withdrawn, and no such separation is taken to license an inference to distinct makers. The Characters are read as an operation, a registry of thirty vices on a single column, legible before any question of persons. The strongest form, one self-dividing maker, with Plato the dialogue position, Theophrastus the first draft and Aristotle the treatise position and legal identity, is stated as a hypothesis.

These readings state what would weaken or decide them: a grammatical sign at the hinge, or an extant Theophrastan work answering the fragment's questions, would falsify the hinge; an independent witness to the partition from outside the Peripatos would weaken the witness reading; Isḥāq's Arabic, read at five loci, would decide among the competing readings of the fragment; and any epigraphic or papyrological item for Theophrastus is listed as still open. What they show concerns what Theophrastus's attestation rests on, and leaves open whether he was a person; they are held as provisional, with no independent uptake.

Compression · Field alone (B)theopheastus

Theophrastus was Aristotle's colleague and successor at the Lyceum, a philosopher and naturalist of whose writings less than a tenth survives; how far he departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part.

👤 The received person

  • Born Tyrtamus, Eresos, c. 371; reputedly renamed by Aristotle for his speech.2↘
    Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school.§1 Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech.§2
  • Successor: Aristotle's library and the school; some 35 years as head.1↘
    Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to the school and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus.§3
  • The will: garden and buildings to the school; the books to Neleus.1↘
    Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to the school and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus.§3

📚 The works

  • 227 titles listed; a small fraction survives.1↘
    Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis.§4
  • Plants: Enquiry and Causes, the counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; 'father of botany'.1↘
    The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany.§5
  • Characters, logic, senses: thirty types; prosleptic syllogisms credited to him; On the Senses an independent work.1↘
    The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work.§6
  • Metaphysics: difficulties for teleology and the unmoved mover.1↘
    His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them.§7

⚖️ How far from Aristotle

  • Only partly determinable: neither footnote nor radical innovator; much known through Alexander and Simplicius.1↘
    How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius.§8

Expansion · Field alone (B)8 sentences · every one sourced below

Theophrastus

Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school. Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech.

Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to the school and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus. Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis.

The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany. The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work. His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them.

How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius.

Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school. Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech. Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to the school and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus. Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis. The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany. The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work. His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them. How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius.

Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher and naturalist, a native of Eresos on Lesbos, and Aristotle's colleague and successor as head of the Lyceum, the Peripatetic school. Born Tyrtamus, he is said to have been renamed by Aristotle for the grace, or the godlike quality, of his speech. Aristotle left him his library and named him successor; under his headship of some thirty-five years the school acquired a more institutionalized character, and his own will, preserved by Diogenes Laertius, left its garden, house and colonnades to be held in common and the books, Aristotle's manuscripts among them, to Neleus. Diogenes lists some 227 titles, more than 232,000 lines, across the whole field of knowledge; of well over two hundred treatises less than a tenth survives, and the corrupt state of what does lends plausibility to the story of the books languishing in a cellar at Scepsis. The surviving works include the Enquiry into Plants, which classifies plants by generation, locality and size, and On the Causes of Plants, the pair described as a counterpart to Aristotle's zoology; after Linnaeus some have called him the father of botany. The Characters, thirty sketches of negative Athenian types, are the first recorded systematic character writing; in logic he is credited with introducing prosleptic syllogisms and with discussing hypothetical ones alongside Eudemus; and On the Senses, long read only as a doxographic source, is now recognized as an independent work. His short Metaphysics raises difficulties for universal teleology and for the unmoved mover, developing problems beyond experience more than solving them. How far he followed or departed from Aristotle can be determined only in part: he is read as neither a footnoting disciple nor a radical innovator, and many of his views have to be reconstructed from later writers such as Alexander of Aphrodisias and Simplicius. A body of work set against that received picture holds that the surviving corpora under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus do not support treating the names as two distinct authors; the number of makers is left open, open because uncounted, and calendar and membership are not claimed. On that reading the received biography is a set of relations supplied by receiving texts, and "Theophrastus" is read as a position within the corpus, the first draft of the Aristotle-position, "first" naming the order of method. Against the received reading of the Metaphysics as a pupil's questions put from outside to Aristotle's Λ, its sixth and seventh sections are read as a hinge written from inside Λ, with no marker at the hinge of a second person taking up a first person's work; at one locus the fragment names Λ 8's object, the number of the spheres, and refuses by name the method Λ has used. A directed measure of rare-term uptake ranks the edge from the fragment to Λ first of 1,482; the two passages are read as standing in ordered dependency at eight locations, and the sequence alone is held unable to decide which was written first. Twelve titles stand letter for letter in both catalogues, one entry assigns a work to "Aristotelian or Theophrastan", and five of Aristotle's lost early dialogues have Theophrastan twins. Theophrastus is also read as void as an independent control for Aristotle: he fails the rule that a control be attested independently of style, doctrine or succession, the two corpora share one transmission channel, and all four kinds of witness to the division between Plato and Aristotle are read as passing through him. The first principal axis of stylistic variation across the two corpora is read as a world/apparatus axis, ahead of any author axis; supervised attribution recovers the names above chance (0.798, against 0.860 for the operation), an earlier claim that they sit at chance was withdrawn, and no such separation is taken to license an inference to distinct makers. The Characters are read as an operation, a registry of thirty vices on a single column, legible before any question of persons. The strongest form, one self-dividing maker, with Plato the dialogue position, Theophrastus the first draft and Aristotle the treatise position and legal identity, is stated as a hypothesis. These readings state what would weaken or decide them: a grammatical sign at the hinge, or an extant Theophrastan work answering the fragment's questions, would falsify the hinge; an independent witness to the partition from outside the Peripatos would weaken the witness reading; Isḥāq's Arabic, read at five loci, would decide among the competing readings of the fragment; and any epigraphic or papyrological item for Theophrastus is listed as still open. What they show concerns what Theophrastus's attestation rests on, and leaves open whether he was a person; they are held as provisional, with no independent uptake.

Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher, naturalist, and the successor to Aristotle as the head of the Peripatetic school (the Lyceum) in Athens. Originally named Tyrtamus, he was given the nickname "Theophrastus"—meaning "he of godlike speech"—by Aristotle due to his remarkable oratorical skills.
While he wrote over 200 treatises covering physics, logic, metaphysics, and ethics, he is most famous today as the "Father of Botany" for establishing the foundational framework of plant science.

Major Surviving Works

Though less than 10% of his massive library of work survives, his extant texts remain deeply influential across multiple fields:
• Enquiry into Plants (Historia Plantarum): A nine-volume biological masterpiece where he classified and described over 500 plant varieties, detailing their geographical distribution, structures, and medicinal properties.
• On the Causes of Plants (De Causis Plantarum): A six-volume counterpart focusing on plant physiology. It explores plant reproduction, cultivation methods, and the direct impacts of climate on crop yields.
• The Characters (Charaktēres): A distinct detour into social and moral psychology. It features 30 brief, humorous, and biting sketches of undesirable human personality traits (such as "The Flatterer," "The Arrogant," and "The Loquacious Man").
• Minor Scientific Treatises: Surviving shorter works include On Fire, On Stones, On Odours, and Weather Signs, the latter earning him a reputation among historians as one of the world's earliest documented weather forecasters.

Core Philosophical & Scientific Contributions

• Empirical Botany: Rather than relying purely on philosophical deduction, Theophrastus observed the natural world directly. He categorized plants systematically by their growth forms (trees, shrubs, undershrubs, and herbs).
• Expanding Logic: Alongside his colleague Eudemus of Rhodes, he advanced the Aristotelian logic system by developing complex hypothetical and modal syllogisms.
• Refining Metaphysics: He challenged aspects of Aristotle’s rigid teleology (the idea that everything in nature exists for a distinct final purpose). Instead, he argued that some natural phenomena occur simply by necessity or coincidence.
